explanations.explanation: Galilee is right, friend. Mark says that after the arrest of John, Jesus went into Galilee and proclaimed the gospel of God (Mark 1:14). John the Baptist had been arrested, and Galilee is where Jesus went next. That's the place Mark names.
Judea is a real region, so I see why it came to mind. But the text says Jesus went into Galilee (Mark 1:14). Judea just isn't the place Mark names here. Easy one to mix up, friend.

Samaria is a real place too, but it's not the one in this verse. Mark says Jesus went into Galilee after John's arrest (Mark 1:14). That's where He proclaims the gospel of God. I once packed a whole box of the wrong cookies, so trust me, mixing up a label is easy.

Yes, friend! Jesus says, "The time is fulfilled…" and "…the kingdom of God is near." (Mark 1:15). He doesn't say it's far off or someday. He says near. That's the kind of news you'd want to hear loud and clear.

A famine would be rough news, but that's not what Jesus says. He says, "…the kingdom of God is near." (Mark 1:15). His message is called the gospel, and that means good news. A famine in the cookie jar is bad enough, so I'm glad that isn't the announcement.

That's a big project, but it's not what Jesus talks about here. He says, "The time is fulfilled…" and "…the kingdom of God is near." (Mark 1:15). Nothing in this passage mentions rebuilding anything. Jesus keeps the focus on the kingdom of God.

explanations.answer: Repent and believe in the gospel
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! Jesus says, "Repent and believe in the gospel!" (Mark 1:15). Two parts, one call. Repent means turning around, and believe means trusting the good news He's announcing.

explanations.answer: Fast and pray at the temple
explanations.explanation: Fasting and praying are good things, but they aren't what Jesus says in this verse. His two-part call is, "Repent and believe in the gospel!" (Mark 1:15). No trip to the temple is mentioned here. Easy to grab the familiar answer, friend, I do it with cookie recipes all the time.

That sounds like a religious to-do list, but it isn't Jesus' call here. He says, "Repent and believe in the gospel!" (Mark 1:15). That's the two parts. Nothing about priests or offerings shows up in these verses.

Right on, friend! Jesus tells Simon and Andrew, "Come, follow Me…" and "…I will make you fishers of men." (Mark 1:17). Simon and Andrew are fishermen, casting a net into the sea, when He says it. I'd have asked what the pay was.

Shepherds of Israel isn't what Jesus says. He says, "…I will make you fishers of men." (Mark 1:17). He's talking to two men with a net in the water. A shepherd's staff wouldn't help them much on that sea.

That's not what Jesus says to them. He says, "…I will make you fishers of men." (Mark 1:17). Simon and Andrew are fishermen when He finds them, casting a net into the sea. So He speaks right in the middle of their work.
True! Mark says, "And at once they left their nets and followed Him." (Mark 1:18). Simon and Andrew leave the nets behind and follow. Mark says they do it at once. That's a quick yes.
Close, but it's true. Mark says, "And at once they left their nets and followed Him." (Mark 1:18). They do leave the nets, and they do follow. I'd still be hunting for my oven mitts.
Mending is right, baker! Mark says James and John "…were in a boat, mending their nets." (Mark 1:19). They're fixing the tools of their trade when Jesus sees them. Then He calls them right away.

Selling isn't what the text says. James and John "…were in a boat, mending their nets." (Mark 1:19). They're working on their nets, not trading anything. No market stand in this scene, friend, just a boat and some netting.
Washing nets sounds believable, friend. But Mark says they were "…mending their nets." (Mark 1:19). Mending means repairing them, and that's the job the text names.

Not quite, friend. Mark says they "…left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and followed Him." (Mark 1:20). So James and John go, and Zebedee is the one who stays. It's the opposite of what the statement says.

False is right! Mark says Jesus called them immediately, and they "…left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and followed Him." (Mark 1:20). James and John go, and Zebedee stays in the boat. Good catch, baker.

The hired men, yes! Mark says James and John left their father Zebedee "…in the boat with the hired men…" (Mark 1:20). So Zebedee isn't left by himself. He has workers right there with him. Hired men, friend, not an empty boat.

A mother is a natural guess, but this passage doesn't mention one. Mark says they left Zebedee "…in the boat with the hired men…" (Mark 1:20). The hired men are the ones named. I'll stick with what the text gives us.
The Pharisees don't show up in this scene. Mark says Zebedee was left "…in the boat with the hired men…" (Mark 1:20). Hired men, not Pharisees. Just working men in a boat.
